author: Tyhuang426e
text:
During the COVID pandemic, the political leader I disliked most was Jacinda Ardern, the former Prime Minister of New Zealand. I disliked her because of what she said to a worldwide television audience.

Facing the flood of confusing information about COVID, she said: “When you see those messages, remember: unless you hear it from us (the government), it is not true. We (the government) will continue to be your single source of truth.”

A reporter asked her: “Are you dividing New Zealand into two classes, the vaccinated and the unvaccinated?” She replied lightly: “Yes, that’s about it.”And yet this person, with such a simple grasp of things, was recently hired as a professor by the University of Sydney! To teach what? “Empathetic leadership,” “social cohesion,” and “civic trust.”

Not only the University of Sydney: Harvard and Oxford have also brought her on. That news wiped out the last scrap of respect I had for university education in the humanities and social sciences.
T
he world is complex. I have lived 70 years and still don’t dare draw conclusions lightly about what happens each day, while a university student’s mind is surely simpler than mine. Simple-minded students paired with equally simple-minded teachers will inevitably become even more simple-minded people!

The first symptom of a simple mind is gullibility. A famous anchor at CNN, a major American TV network, is a typical case. Not long ago, she interviewed the current US Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the two clashed fiercely over COVID:

Kennedy Jr.: “I know you’re getting a little nervous right now.”

CNN anchor (Dana Bash): “I’m not nervous at all.”

Kennedy Jr.: “Do you think your job is to dispel the public’s doubts about vaccines, or to tell the American people the truth?”

Dana Bash: “I think my job is to tell the truth. And the truth is that there are study after study, countless scientific studies. This is one of the most thoroughly researched areas in science.”

Kennedy Jr.: “You’re just parroting those lines. You’re like a parrot. I’ve actually read those scientific reports. Why don’t you come back here with me some time and we’ll debate those studies properly?”

Dana Bash: “I’m not going to debate you on this topic.”

Kennedy Jr.: “Of course you won’t. All you ever do is repeat what you’re told and say ‘trust the experts.’ That’s what you did during COVID. And now we all know that the so-called expert, Anthony Fauci, was lying about everything, whether it was masks, social distancing, natural immunity, the vaccines’ ability to block transmission, or the origin of the virus. He was lying, and you were punishing the people who didn’t trust the experts. Now you’re trotting out the expert routine again, to talk about a field you personally know nothing about.”

This journalist’s mind is as simple as the former New Zealand Prime Minister’s: they trusted the judgments of government experts and used their power and influence to steer everyone into a farce of overtreating a minor illness. I checked, and both the journalist and the former Prime Minister studied in the humanities and social sciences, in almost the same major: politics and media.

At 70, I no longer write for readers; I write to warn my descendants. I hope they will not study the humanities and social sciences at university. Why?

First, in the internet age, a university degree in the humanities and social sciences has lost its value.Before the internet, studying these fields at university served three purposes: listening to lecturers, using the library, and making friends. Now the internet has completely overturned or replaced all three. Why spend so much money and time on an arts degree?

Second, studying these fields is not only a waste of money and effort; it also tends to wash the mind into something simple and extreme.
Besides making people easy to deceive, a simple mind in politics very easily slides to the left, full of blind righteousness and an urge to change the world. That is why the vast majority of people who march in the streets and block traffic by sitting on main roads are arts students.
In American universities, more than 90% of professors who donate to political parties give to the Democrats, and the share is even higher among professors in the humanities and social sciences. Australian universities have no such official statistics, but judging by the University of Sydney’s hiring of this former New Zealand Prime Minister, the picture is probably not much different. Western universities have now become strongholds of the left, and a child who goes in to study these fields is very likely to be assimilated into the left by graduation.
Why don’t I want my descendants to become leftists?

I came across a widely circulated “left versus right” comparison online. After reading it, I became even more determined to warn my descendants:

On guns: A right-winger who dislikes guns doesn’t buy one. A left-winger who dislikes guns wants to ban everyone else’s.

On diet: A right-winger who is a vegetarian doesn’t eat meat himself. A left-winger who is a vegetarian wants to start a social movement to boycott all animal protein products.

On sex orientation: A right-winger who is gay quietly gets on with his own life. A left-winger who is gay keeps badgering others and forces all of society to publicly declare respect for him.

On unemployment: A right-winger who loses his job figures out how to improve himself, get out of trouble, and make a comeback. A left-winger who loses his job immediately files a complaint, accusing society of discriminating against him.

On arguments: A right-winger who dislikes the opinions on television turns it off or changes the channel. A left-winger who dislikes certain opinions wants to sue the speaker, or even accuse them of defamation.

On faith: A right-winger who is not religious doesn’t go to church or the mosque. A left-winger who is not religious wants to erase all mention of God or religion from the public sphere (except Islam).

On healthcare: A right-winger who needs medical care goes to a doctor and pays for the medicine. A left-winger who needs medical care calls on everyone to unite so that taxpayers share the cost.

On the economy: When the economy is bad, a right-winger tells himself it’s time to roll up his sleeves and work harder. A left-winger tells himself that filthy bosses are bleeding the country dry and the workers are innocent victims.

The ultimate test: when a right-winger finishes reading this comparison, he forwards it to friends and everyone shares a laugh. When a left-winger finishes reading it, he will never forward it, and will instead denounce it indignantly as “misinformation” from a far-right fascist.

Why shouldn’t my descendants become leftists?
Because the left’s greatest obsession is always trying to change other people.

I lived to 70 before I truly understood this: people who are always trying to change others will never be happy in their lives, because it is a task that can never be completed.

Old people talk too much. Let me add one more superfluous remark: I studied economics and taught business management at university. Among the arts and social science disciplines, these are two of the harder ones, and with the internet, neither needs a university degree, let alone the rest.

In an effort to reclaim my two granddaughters from being brainwashed by Australian education, I have specifically recommended fourteen must-read books to them — books that cover content Australian schools don't teach. Both the Chinese and English editions of this book are available on Amazon: "Fourteen Must-Read Books: A Grandfather's Letters to His Australian Granddaughters."
